name: Macassar oil
lead: Macassar oil was a scented compound hair oil used mainly by men in Western Europe in the 19th and early 20th centuries to condition and style hair.[1] It was popularised by the London barber Alexander Rowland, who from about 1793 sold Rowland's Macassar Oil, one of the first nationally advertised products.[1] Advertisements made broad claims, including promoting hair regrowth.[1]

Its name refers to the port of Makassar in Sulawesi, where ingredients were reputedly bought.[1] The oil was greasy enough to stain furniture, which led to the antimacassar, a washable cloth protecting chair backs.[1]
infobox: Originally Macassar ebony or kusum oil; later coconut, palm or other vegetable oils with ylang-ylang[1]

paras: Wikipedia reports it was first made from oil of Macassar ebony, later from Schleichera oleosa (kusum) oil; as the tree became scarce, makers shifted to vegetable oils such as coconut or palm, often blended with ylang-ylang for fragrance.[1] Grokipedia gives a similar account, adding that alcohol and castor oil were used in some formulations.[2]

Rowland began selling the oil around 1793, and the family firm registered the name as a trademark in 1888.[1] Advertising claimed regrowth for balding men; a c.1814 Thomas Rowlandson illustration satirised such claims, and Lord Byron and Lewis Carroll referred to the oil in their writing.[1]
Alternatives such as brilliantine, pomade and Brylcreem later became common.[1]
No studies found. A 1998 patent application describes a method of extracting Macassar oil from Schleichera trijuga seeds for use as a cosmetic hair and scalp agent, but it is not a clinical study.[3]

timeline.event: Alexander Rowland begins selling Rowland's Macassar Oil.[1]
The Rowland firm registers the name as a trademark.[1]

card.summary: The Victorian hair oil that gave us the antimacassar; historically marketed for growth and styling, with no clinical evidence behind the growth claims.
card.note: Historical product; regrowth claims were advertising claims and have not been studied.

quick.overview:
Macassar oil was a perfumed vegetable-based hair oil popular with men in the 1800s. Alexander Rowland sold it from about 1793 and advertised it widely.

Its grease on chair backs gave rise to the antimacassar cloth.
quick.mechanism: It was a plain emollient hair dressing that coated and smoothed hair; advertised effects on growth have not been studied.
quick.risks: No specific harms are documented in the available sources. Its main historical drawback was staining of upholstery.
